1.q: הוֹד֣וּ לַ⁠יהוָ֣ה כִּי־ט֑וֹב כִּ֖י לְ⁠עוֹלָ֣ם חַסְדּֽ⁠וֹ
1.note: See how you translated these same phrases in Psalm 106:1.

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea here and throughout this psalm in another way. Alternate translation: [the way he is faithful to his covenant]

2.note: The term “god,” when applied to a being other than Yahweh, can refer to an idol, but, as here, it can also refer to any lesser spirit being. Alternate translation: [to the God who is above any other spiritual being]

Here and throughout the psalm where this phrase is repeated, the psalmist is using **to forever** as a common expression of his culture to mean “eternally” or “without end.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for his covenant faithfulness lasts forever]

3.note: The psalmist is using this possessive form to mean that Yahweh is the supreme Lord, greater than all other rulers. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the Lord who is above all other lords]

4.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Give thanks to the one doing great wonders]

5.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Give thanks to the one making the heavens]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **understanding**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [To the one who skillfully made the heavens]

6.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Give thanks to the one spreading out the earth]

7.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Give thanks to the one making great lights]

8.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [who made the sun for dominion in the day]

The psalmist speaks of **the sun** as if it were a king that could have **dominion** or rule over the day. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the sun to give light in the day]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **dominion**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to govern]

9.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [who made the moon and stars for dominion in the night]

The psalmist speaks of **the moon and stars** as if they were kings that could have **dominion** or rule over the night. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the moon and stars to give light in the night]

10.note: Here, **striker** represents one who kills. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [To the one who killed the Egyptian’s firstborn]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Give thanks to the one striking Egypt]
Here, **Egypt** represents the people of Egypt. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the Egyptians]

11.note: Here, **Israel** represents the people of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel]
The pronoun **their** refers to the Egyptians. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the midst of the Egyptians]

12.note: The terms **a strong hand** and **an outstretched arm** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [By his very great power]

Here, **strong hand** and **outstretched arm** both represent the power of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [By his mighty power]

13.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Give thanks to the one parting the Sea of Reeds]

14.note: Here, **Israel** represents the people of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel]
The pronoun **it** refers to the Sea of Reeds. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the midst of the Sea of Reeds]

16.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Give thanks to the one leading his people]

17.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Give thanks to the one striking great kings]

Here, **striking** represents killing, defeating, or conquering. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [To the one conquering]

19.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [He conquered Sihon, king of the Amorite]

20.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and he killed Og, king of the Bashan]

21.note: The pronoun **their** refers to the defeated kings, Sihon and Og. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the land of those kings]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **inheritance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for the Israelites to inherit]

22.note: Here, **Israel his servant** represents the people of Israel who served Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to the Israelites, his servants]
Here the pronoun **his** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s servant]

23.note: Here the psalmist shifts from speaking about Israel in the third person to speaking as one of the Israelites, using the pronouns **our** and **us**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could maintain a consistent perspective. Alternate translation: [who, when his people were humbled, remembered them]

The pronoun **who** refers to Yahweh, while the pronoun **our** refers to the Israelites. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [even when we Israelites were humiliated, Yahweh]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **humiliation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [who, when we were humbled]

24.note: Here the psalmist is speaking of Yahweh saving his people as if he physically **tore** them away from their enemies, as one would tear an object from the grip of another person. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he rescued us from our adversaries]

25.note: Here the psalmist does not explicitly state who the one **giving**. The subject is Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, who gives bread to all of flesh]
The psalmist is using one kind of food, **bread**, to mean food in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [food]

The psalmist is using **all of flesh** to represent all living creatures. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to everyone]
